title: Jubilee 2000
hook: churches campaigned to cancel poor countries' debts, citing Leviticus 25

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hospice, and a nurse who refused to let the dying be left alone. Your line was you matter to the end. Who came to mind when you heard it? Day nine hundred ninety-seven.

Fifty years, then a trumpet. In the book of Leviticus, Israel is told to count seven times seven years, and then, on the day of atonement, to sound the trumpet through the whole land. What follows is a startling law. A field sold in a bad year goes back to the family that lost it. People who had sold themselves into service go home. The board is reset. Much later, churches and aid groups picked up that trumpet and pointed it at something modern: the debts weighing on poor countries. They named their campaign after the old law. Today, Jubilee 2000, and the law that gave it a name.

The law is in Leviticus 25. The fiftieth year is to be holy, and the King James Bible gives the command: "proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you." Liberty, for a whole land, on a timetable. The reason behind the law comes a few verses on, spoken by God: "for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me." Nobody owns the ground forever. Everyone is a guest on it. So wealth can pile up for a while, but not for good. Deuteronomy has a smaller cousin of the same idea: "At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release," a letting go of debts between neighbors. Here is the honest part. Leviticus gives the jubilee law, and some readers note that the rest of the Bible tells no story of one being kept. The idea kept traveling anyway. In Luke, Jesus reads from Isaiah in his hometown and announces "the acceptable year of the Lord," and some readers hear a jubilee in it. And Christians who pray the Lord's Prayer in Matthew's words say: "forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." Then came the campaign. Christian groups, joined by people of other faiths and none, argued that old loans were pressing on countries that could barely pay for their own clinics and schools, and that a fresh start was owed. They gathered signatures, held vigils, and marched. Some debts were later written off. Others were not, and people still argue, inside churches and outside them, about what helped and what didn't. But a line from an ancient law about farmland had walked into the rooms where finance ministers meet.
screen: `THE LAND IS MINE: YOU ARE GUESTS.`
`AN OLD LAW IN THE FINANCE MINISTRY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the trumpet sound once, quietly. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a debt in your own life, and not only money. Something you owe, or something someone owes you, that has sat on the table a long time. Hold it without adding it up. Then widen the circle: a neighbor, a family, a country carrying something it cannot lift. If you pray, you can pray the line from Matthew: forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. If you don't, just let the word release sit with you. After the bell, take a few minutes to read how debt relief works, from more than one side. The bell holds the time.
Jubilee 2000. A campaign, carried by churches among others, to cancel the debts of poor countries, named for the jubilee of Leviticus 25: the year when what was lost goes home.
Your line: proclaim liberty. Today, let go of one small thing someone owes you, a favor, an apology, a few dollars, and don't mention that you did. Day nine hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Churches and Christian aid groups campaign and pray for debt relief for poor countries, often drawing on the jubilee of Leviticus 25 and the line "forgive us our debts" from the Lord's Prayer.

fork.reveal: Leviticus 25: in the jubilee, every man returns to his possession. the reason given is surprising: the land was never anyone's to sell forever. "the land is mine."

original.note: Hebrew: the word Leviticus 25 uses for the fiftieth year, the jubilee.

trapdoor: what you thought: a jubilee is a big anniversary party.
what it means: a year of release in Leviticus 25. land goes home, people go home, and everyone starts again, because the land belongs to God.
what a scholar hears: Leviticus gives the law, and some readers note no story of it being kept. the idea travels on anyway, into Luke 4, the Lord's Prayer, and a modern campaign about debt.

notes: Claims rule: 'seven times seven years', 'fiftieth year' and 'the day of atonement' are from Leviticus 25:8–10 directly. No dates, counts of signatures, countries or amounts of debt are given for the campaign.

Liberty Bell: the bell carries the Leviticus 25:10 line ('Proclaim LIBERTY Throughout all the Land unto all the Inhabitants thereof Lev. XXV X.'). This is not in the cited text; confirm it may stay, or cut.
'the Bible never describes Israel actually celebrating one': the standard scholarly observation (Jeremiah 34 concerns a seventh-year release of slaves, not a jubilee). Confirm wording.
'some readers hear a jubilee in it' (Luke 4:19): attributed, not stated as fact. Confirm.

Campaign summary kept general: churches and aid groups, people of other faiths and none, signatures, vigils, marches; 'some debts were later written off, others were not' and ongoing argument. Confirm fair; the campaign's specific outcomes (e.g. HIPC, MDRI) are deliberately not named.
Original: יוֹבֵל (yovel). Its link to the ram's horn is left out under the etymology rule.

Editor pass: cut the Liberty Bell line (not in the cited text); softened 'the Bible never describes Israel celebrating one' to an attributed 'some readers note' in teach and trapdoor; replaced the myth item that rested on that claim with one about the fiftieth year (Lev 25:8–10, Deut 15:1).
